leads.why_a_lead: Runner-up (2nd place) in Casey Trees' Aug 2023 citizen-science DC big-tree contest, right behind the Battery Kemble chestnut oak (wdc_003) which won overall. Reported by Washingtonian and City Cast DC (both already used as sources for wdc_003) but neither gives exact in-arboretum location, measurements or an age estimate for this specific tree; would need a dedicated search of the Arboretum's own visitor materials or a call to Casey Trees for the submission record. National Arboretum transit checked this pass: ~16 min by WMATA bus from downtown (Massachusetts Av NE+1 St NE to 21 Pl NE+Maryland Av NE) or DC Streetcar from Union Station, both comfortably inside the ~30 min day-trip boundary, so the site itself is not a blocker. The Arboretum overall is a very strong hunting ground for future passes (huge Asian collection, National Bonsai & Penjing Museum, Capitol Columns) but needs its own dedicated search; this pass only surfaced the single willow oak via the big-tree contest coverage.

leads.candidate: Dumbarton Oaks / Dumbarton Oaks Park veteran trees, Georgetown
leads.why_a_lead: Dumbarton Oaks (the museum garden) documents 182 trees including a 'last remaining pre-Bliss oak' by the Museum Shop (40in diameter, no age given) and has run a 2023-24 photo exhibition specifically on its oldest trees (Sahar Coston-Hardy, text drawn from Beatrix Farrand's Plant Book), which strongly suggests individually documented specimens with ages exist in Dumbarton Oaks' own archives/plant books but were not surfaced by open web search this pass. Dumbarton Oaks Park (the wilder, NPS-managed section down the valley) is a separate, free, fully public site and a promising second angle. Worth a dedicated pass: search doaks.org library-archives plant lists directly, and check whether the museum garden (paid entry) vs. the park (free, public) affects which specific trees would even qualify under the access bar.

leads.candidate: Andrew Jackson Magnolia(s), White House South Portico
leads.why_a_lead: Reportedly planted 1829 by President Jackson in memory of his wife Rachel, depicted on the old $20 bill, and part of the same NPS HALS Witness Tree Protection Program as wdc_001/wdc_004/wdc_006 (so a dedicated HALS report likely exists, not yet located this pass). NOT pursued as a verified entry because: (1) one of the two trees was removed in 2017 for poor health and replaced with a sapling grown from its seed, so at most ONE of the two current trees could be the historic original, and this pass could not confirm which; (2) the White House South Lawn is not general public access, and it is unverified this pass whether the tree(s) are visible/photographable from the public Ellipse or E Street, or only from inside ticketed tours. Needs both a health/identity check (is the surviving tree the pre-2017 original or itself a replacement) and an access check before it could ever ship, per hard rule 10 on withheld/restricted locations.

leads.candidate: White mulberry / catalpa / Amur cork tree ensembles from the same HALS Witness Tree Protection Program (DC-8 East Potomac cherries, catalpas at Survey Lodge Ranger Station, willow oak circle south of the Vietnam Women's Memorial, Amur cork trees near the FDR Memorial, multiple varieties at the DC War Memorial)
leads.why_a_lead: All part of the same 24-tree 2006 HALS survey that produced wdc_001, wdc_004 and wdc_006 (three of our strongest, best-documented entries this pass), so the remaining ~18 trees in that survey are a very efficient target for a future pass: same documentation quality, same NPS ownership, same National Mall/Union Square walkability. Not pursued individually this pass for time reasons and because several are explicitly plural/ensemble ('catalpa trees', 'Amur cork trees', a 'circle of willow oak trees') and would need a collectible-point judgement call (compact named ensemble vs. an avenue/wood, which is blocked per the rules) that a full HALS PDF read would resolve. The DC-8 Yoshino cherries at East Potomac Golf Course near Hains Point are also documented as having 'hollow condition of most principal branches consistent with past insect infestation', a health flag worth checking before pursuit. A future pass should pull the full 24-tree HALS index from loc.gov (search 'habshaer dc1000' sequential item numbers dc1032 through roughly dc1050) rather than re-discovering trees one at a time via web search.
